description:
We’re Menasim to the Moon, a multidisciplinary team formed through MENASIM, a nonprofit that brings engineers and other professionals together to tackle environmental challenges.

Our team combines experience in aerospace engineering, remote sensing, data and AI, software development, product and UX, and 3D visualization.

For the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge, we’re developing Moon Watchers: an intuitive, visually engaging tool for exploring lunar missions and landing conditions. Our goal is to make complex lunar data accessible and support informed, environmentally responsible exploration of the Moon.
summary:
Moon Watchers is a web app that helps mission planners compare landing sites and dates near the Moon’s south pole. A team planning a solar-powered lander can see when each site receives sunlight, when its chosen ground station is visible, and how shifting the landing date changes those windows.

Users can choose from 30 catalogued sites, select a point on the map, or draw a region to rank locations within it. They can set the landing date, mission duration, solar panel and antenna heights, and assign weights to sunlight, communication access, and terrain slope. Each site card plots the paths of the Sun and Earth against the local terrain horizon. A timeline shows how conditions change throughout the mission.

A Python engine uses NASA lunar mapping, LOLA terrain data, and JPL SPICE ephemerides to calculate viewing conditions from 84°S to 90°S. An AI guide turns plain-language requests into site cards and explains the results.

Our team, Menasim to the Moon, also considered how lunar dust affects mobility and equipment. The app includes a separate regolith layer whose current coverage extends from 70°S to 70°N.
details:
Goal: Moon Watchers answers two fundamental questions for any landing site near the lunar south pole: When will the lander have access to sunlight, and when can it communicate directly with Earth? It then helps mission planners compare landing sites and dates and quickly adapt to changes in mission schedules, design, and operational requirements.

Site Calculator: Each site card represents a customizable mission scenario. Users can select one of 30 catalogued landing sites (including Artemis III candidate regions, massifs, crater rims, and crater floors) or any custom location within the lunar south polar region (84°S to 90°S). Mission parameters include the landing date and time (UTC), mission duration (1–365 days), solar panel and antenna heights (1–10 m), and one or more Earth-based ground stations, either selected from a catalogue (NASA’s Deep Space Network or ESA’s ESTRACK) or defined using custom coordinates.

Live Dynamic Status: At any moment during the mission, each site card shows whether the site is sunlit and whether ground station contact is available. It also displays the Sun’s and Earth’s elevation angles, the terrain horizon elevation in their respective directions, angular clearance (the difference between the two elevation angles), and countdowns to sunset, sunrise, Earthset, and Earthrise. A shared time slider with a playback option allows users to advance through the mission timeline across all sites simultaneously, with independent time controls planned for future versions.

Ridge Graph: Displays the local terrain horizon (the highest apparent ridge in every azimuth direction) alongside the Sun’s and Earth’s apparent paths throughout the mission (default 29.5 days), allowing users to understand why and when a site loses sunlight or communication. It also includes important scientific explanations and interactive exploration of latitude and longitude through the map.

Map: An interactive lunar south polar map based on the Mean Earth (ME) reference frame and NASA LOLA data, with layers for terrain relief, permanently shadowed regions (PSRs), Earth contact, terrain slope, a simulated lunar regolith index, and lunar libration. Users can click anywhere within the supported region to add a new site for analysis.

Polygon Analysis: Users can outline a region of interest manually or with the assistance of the AI guide and select a grid resolution of 2, 5, or 10 km. Each grid cell is evaluated by the underlying Python calculation engine and scored according to customizable, mission-specific requirements. The highest-scoring locations are ranked and can be opened as individual site cards for further analysis.

Customized Score: an illustrative 0–100 grade from seven factors (sunlight, station contact, longest darkness, longest outage, sunlight at landing, slope, lunar regolith), with the breakdown and the deciding factor. Users can change the weights to match their spacecraft's needs.

Side by side Timelines: a Gantt view of sunlight, Earth contact, their overlap and unknown terrain for every site on a shared mission-day axis, plus a side-by-side comparison table below.

Orbit: a 3D lunar globe showing the Sun's and Earth's directions for any date and hour.

AI Guide: Users can enter plain-language requests such as “a four-month mission near Shackleton starting in March 2027.” The AI guide (powered by Google Gemini, using the user’s own API key) configures site cards, explains any numerical result, button, or warning based on the app’s own calculations and scientific reference notes, asks follow-up questions when details are missing, suggests score weights based on mission priorities, and opens the polygon analysis tool. It never performs the physical calculations itself. This makes the system accessible to non-experts while maintaining the flexibility and customization required by experienced mission planners and engineers.

Shareable: All scenario parameters are encoded directly in the URL, allowing users to easily share, save, and reload mission scenarios or undo changes using the browser’s Back button.

Metrics and score: Sun %, contact %, overlap, longest darkness and outage, sunlight at landing, and a weighted score with hard gates for steep slopes and permanently shadowed regions as well as lunar regolith.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

  • Faster decision-making: Compare landing sites, landing dates, and equipment heights within seconds.
  • Rapid response to schedule changes: Adjust the landing date or mission duration, extend the mission by a lunar day, or identify more suitable nearby locations and immediately assess the impact.
  • Different missions, different priorities: Adjustable weights allow a power-hungry rover and a communication-critical lander to rank the same landing sites differently, according to their specific mission requirements.
  • Also, accessible to non-experts with LLM assistant
  • Scientific understanding and accessibility: The ridge graph, accompanied by scientific explanations, illustrates why a difference of just a few kilometres or days can significantly affect mission conditions at the lunar south pole, making the tool valuable for educators, the general public, and mission planners alike.
  • Transparency and reliable results: Missing or unavailable data are explicitly marked as unknown rather than replaced with unsupported estimates.
